title: Paint systems, primers and coverage
audience: Painters and painting workers who select paint systems and estimate coverage
learningOutcomes: Select a primer and topcoat that are compatible with each other and with the substrate.
Estimate coverage from the product data sheet and the surface area, and allow for the surface type.
Apply the product in the conditions stated on the data sheet.

instruction.heading: What a paint system is
instruction.body: A paint system is the set of products that go on a surface in a set order: a primer or sealer, sometimes an undercoat, and a topcoat. Each layer has a job. A primer or sealer is chosen to bond to the substrate, to seal a porous or absorbent surface, to block stains, or to stop a substrate from reacting with the paint above it. An undercoat builds body and evens out colour. A topcoat gives the finish, the colour and most of the durability. Each layer must be compatible with the layer beneath it and with the substrate, meaning the surface the paint goes onto. Products from different manufacturers, or from different chemical families such as water-based and solvent-based, are not always interchangeable over one another. Some primers are made for bare timber, others for plaster, metal, masonry or previously painted surfaces. A system that works on one substrate can fail on another, so the choice is made from the data sheets for the products, not from habit or from the shelf.

instruction.heading: Reading the data sheet before you buy
instruction.body: The product data sheet is the manufacturer's statement of how the product is meant to be used. Before you choose a system, read the data sheet for each layer and check the substrates it is suited to, its compatibility statements, and any warning about what it must not be applied over. Note the recoat window, which is the time that must pass before the next coat can go on, and the drying time to touch and to handle. Check the stated application conditions, including air and surface temperature, humidity and any limits on direct sun or wind. Note the coverage figure, the film thickness it is quoted at, and the number of coats the system needs. Check the solvent or thinner the product uses, the tools it needs, and the personal protection the safety data sheet requires. Record the product name, the batch number and the data sheet reference on the job record, because a fault that is traced to a batch cannot be investigated without them.

instruction.heading: Water-based, solvent-based and over old finishes
instruction.body: Mixing water-based and solvent-based products is a common cause of poor adhesion, lifting and wrinkling. Some water-based topcoats do not bond well to an old gloss or oil-based finish, which is glossy and non-porous, so the surface may need to be scuffed, cleaned and fitted with a bonding primer or another compatible system before the topcoat. The data sheet names what it is compatible with, and where it does not name the substrate or the previous finish, do not assume compatibility. A small test patch, left for the time the data sheet gives, is a practical check on a job where the old finish is unknown. Record the test and its result. Do not thin a topcoat or change its system to make it go on more easily unless the data sheet allows it.

instruction.heading: Substrate types and what they change
instruction.body: Timber needs sealing of knots and resins, and a primer that suits bare timber. Plaster and new plasterboard often need a sealer to stop the surface from absorbing paint unevenly and to control the sheen. Bare metal may need a rust-inhibiting primer that suits the metal and the environment. Masonry and render can be alkaline and damp, so the primer must suit that. Previously painted surfaces need checking for gloss, chalking, flaking and whether the old paint is sound, because the new system can only be as good as the surface under it. Each substrate has its own primer in the data sheet, and the choice of primer is recorded on the system record.

instruction.heading: Coverage: how much paint to buy
instruction.body: Coverage is the area that one litre of paint covers at the film thickness the manufacturer states. The figure on the data sheet is usually quoted for a smooth, sound surface under stated conditions. Rough, porous and textured surfaces take more paint, so the quantity needs an allowance for the surface type. Begin by measuring the area to be painted: multiply the length and height of each wall, add the other surfaces, and subtract openings that will not be painted. Multiply the area by the number of coats the system needs. Divide by the coverage figure from the data sheet to find the litres needed, then add an allowance for surface and waste. Round up to the nearest container size the product comes in. As a worked example only, with invented numbers: a wall of 40 square metres, two coats, a data sheet figure of 12 square metres per litre, and a 15 per cent allowance gives 80 square metres of coverage needed, which is 6.67 litres, plus 15 per cent, about 7.7 litres, so the job would order 8 litres of that product. Use the data sheet and the site's own figures for the real job.

instruction.heading: Application conditions and recoat times
instruction.body: Each coat should go on in the conditions the data sheet states. Paint applied in cold, damp, very hot or windy conditions can dry too fast, too slowly, or with a poor film. Painting in direct sun can make the paint dry before it levels, and the dark surfaces heat up faster. Check the surface temperature as well as the air temperature where the data sheet asks for it. Do not recoat before the previous coat has dried for the time the data sheet gives, because a second coat applied too early can lift or soften the first coat. A recoat window that runs out may need the surface to be lightly abraded or cleaned before the next coat, as the data sheet directs. Record the conditions at the time of application.

instruction.heading: Check the licence position before the job starts
instruction.body: The value of the job can decide whether a painting licence or registration is needed, and the test differs by state. New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). Materials count towards that value. Western Australia: painting work valued at $1,000 or more requires a licence, which is painting contractor registration (WA Government painters' scope of work page, last updated 23 December 2025). Victoria: painting-only jobs need no registration. You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills, such as plastering and painting, to complete a job (Consumer Victoria registration page, last updated 9 July 2025). Queensland: the licence position for painting-only work is not confirmed by an official source. South Australia, Tasmania, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory: the licence position for painting is not confirmed by an official source. Check the position for your state before you buy the materials or accept the job, and check it again if the scope grows.

instruction.heading: The limits of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson does not give a painting licence, a contractor licence or authority to undertake regulated building work. Completing it does not make you competent to select systems for substrates you have not been trained on, and the product data sheets always take priority over this lesson.

procedure: Identify each substrate and its condition, including any previous finish, gloss, chalking or damp.
Select a primer and topcoat that the data sheets show are compatible with each other and with the substrate. Where the data sheets do not confirm compatibility, run a test patch or refer.
Measure the area to be painted, subtract openings, and multiply by the number of coats.
Estimate the quantity from the data sheet coverage figure, with an allowance for the surface type and waste, and round up to a container size.
Check the application conditions and the recoat window on the data sheet against the planned work.
Check the licence position for the job's value and state before ordering materials or committing to the job.
Record the product names, batch numbers, data sheet references, the quantity estimate and the conditions at each application.

workedExamples.situation: A timber door is to be painted over an old gloss finish, and the supplier offers a water-based topcoat without a primer.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the water-based topcoat alone a suitable system?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not assume it is. Check the topcoat's data sheet for what it is compatible with over an old gloss finish. An old gloss surface can prevent a water-based topcoat from bonding, so a bonding primer, a scuff and clean, or another compatible system may be required. Test a small patch if the data sheet allows it, record the result, and record the system and the data sheet reference chosen. If the data sheet does not confirm the topcoat alone, the system includes the primer.

workedExamples.situation: A client wants a rough-textured exterior render to have two coats of a topcoat, and the quote was calculated from the smooth-wall coverage figure on the data sheet.
workedExamples.reasoning: Probably not. The coverage figure is for a smooth surface, and render takes more paint. Recalculate with an allowance for the surface type, using the site's own test area where possible. For example only, if a test patch shows the render takes noticeably more paint than the data sheet figure, the quantity is increased to match that result, and the test and the new figure are recorded before ordering.

workedExamples.situation: A job is booked for midday in full sun, on a dark fascia that has just been cleaned, and the forecast shows a hot afternoon.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Does the job go ahead at midday as planned?
workedExamples.reasoning: Check the data sheet's application conditions before going ahead. Sun on a dark surface can heat it beyond the stated limit, causing the paint to dry before it levels. Plan to paint in the shade or later in the day, or in the morning, as the data sheet permits. Record the surface and air conditions at the time of application, and record any change to the plan.

equipmentAndPpe: Product data sheets for each layer of the system, kept with the job record
Safety data sheets for each product, with the protection they require
Measuring tape or laser measure to calculate area
Calculator and the job's quantity estimate form
Thermometer for air and surface temperature, where the data sheet requires it
Eye protection and gloves suitable for the product
Respiratory protection for solvent-based products, used as the SDS specifies, with a fit check
Ventilation, and fire-safe storage for solvent-soaked rags, as the SDS specifies

commonErrors.error: Mixing products from different systems or chemical families without checking compatibility.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the data sheets for each layer and for the substrate. Test a patch where the data sheets are silent.

commonErrors.error: Estimating coverage from the smooth-surface figure for a rough or porous surface.
commonErrors.prevention: Apply an allowance for the surface type and the number of coats, and test where possible.

commonErrors.error: Recoating before the previous coat has dried for the time the data sheet gives.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the drying and recoat times on the data sheet, and check the surface by touch as the sheet directs.

commonErrors.error: Thinning the product or changing the system because it is easier to apply.
commonErrors.prevention: Change nothing that the data sheet does not allow, and record any change that the data sheet permits.

commonErrors.error: Ordering quantities from memory or without an allowance.
commonErrors.prevention: Work from the area, the coats, the coverage figure and an allowance, and record the estimate.

commonErrors.error: Applying paint in sun, wind, cold or damp outside the stated conditions.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the conditions before starting, and reschedule if they are outside the data sheet limits.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Painting licence positions for the job's value: New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). Stand-alone contracts for internal paintwork have not needed one since 2015 unless the paintwork is part of other home building work. Western Australia: painting work valued at $1,000 or more requires a licence, which is painting contractor registration (WA Government painters' scope of work page, last updated 23 December 2025). Victoria: painting-only jobs need no registration. You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills, such as plastering and painting, to complete a job (Consumer Victoria registration page, last updated 9 July 2025). Queensland: the licence position for painting-only work is not confirmed by an official source. South Australia, Tasmania, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory: the licence position for painting is not confirmed by an official source.

The model WHS duties require the supplier to provide a safety data sheet with each hazardous chemical, and the business to identify, assess and control the risks of the chemicals it uses (Safe Work Australia, WHS duties related to hazardous chemicals; checked 2026-11-03). Read the SDS before opening solvent-based products, and follow the ventilation and personal protection it specifies.
Completing this lesson does not give a painting or contractor licence, or any authority to undertake regulated building work.

qualityStandard: The paint system is compatible across layers and with the substrate, and the data sheet reference for each layer is recorded.
The quantity is estimated from the data sheet coverage figure, with the area, the coats and a stated allowance shown.
Each coat is applied within the stated conditions and recoat window, and the conditions are recorded.
documentationEvidence: Paint system record with each product, its batch number, its data sheet reference and any test-patch result.
Quantity estimate showing the area, the coats, the coverage figure and the allowance used.
Application record with the date, the air and surface temperature, the conditions, the drying time and the recoat time for each coat.
Licence position check showing the state, the job value and the date checked.
summary: Check each layer and the substrate for compatibility before choosing the system, and test where the data sheets are silent.
Estimate coverage from the data sheet figure, with an allowance for the surface type, the coats and waste.
Apply each coat within the conditions and recoat window on the data sheet, and record them.

knowledgeChecks.question: A water-based topcoat is to be applied over an old gloss finish without a primer. What is correct?
options: Apply it because the topcoat is the finish and should go on straight away at the job
Check the data sheets and use a compatible system, such as a bonding primer, before applying
Thin the topcoat to improve adhesion on the old finish before the first coat goes on
Apply it in the rain, since the moisture will help the topcoat to cure properly

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must coverage be estimated with an allowance for the surface type?
options: Smooth surfaces take more paint than rough ones do
The surface type does not change the quantity needed
Rough and porous surfaces take more paint than smooth ones
Only the colour changes the quantity of paint needed

knowledgeChecks.question: What does a product's coverage figure describe?
options: The area one litre covers at the stated film thickness
The price of the product per square metre of the wall
The drying time of the product on a standard day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why are the application conditions on the data sheet checked before painting?
options: Paint colour shifts with temperature in every case
Conditions change drying and film quality
Whether it is a licence condition is not confirmed by an official source
